summary: ArtemisForge is a web-based Lunar Landing Site Navigator and Surface Pathfinder built for the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. Landing near the Moon's south pole is extremely hard: the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above the horizon, Earth's libration makes it dip below the horizon and cut communications, and permanently shadowed regions drop to 40 K. ArtemisForge turns raw NASA data into decisions anyone can read. Users explore CLPS landing sites on an interactive 3D Moon, inspect 360° horizon profiles derived from LRO LOLA altimetry, see Sun and Earth elevations with sunset and Earthset countdowns, compare launch slips and alternative sites for power and Direct-to-Earth communication windows, and plan rover routes over real terrain, then export PDF reports. Sun and Earth positions come from the JPL DE421 ephemeris and match JPL Horizons within 0.006°. It serves mission architects, scientists, educators and the public.
details:
What it does. ArtemisForge is a multi-page web app with six tools. (1) Globe Explorer: a 3D Moon with CLPS mission pins (IM-1, IM-2, Griffin-1, IM-4, Blue Moon MK1, Blue Ghost and others), the solar terminator and the Earth direction. (2) Site Analysis: a 360° horizon panorama and polar dome from LRO LOLA elevation data, Sun and Earth elevation and azimuth, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, day/night and Earth-visibility timelines, and PDF export of four-layer site maps. (3) Scenario Compare: side-by-side evaluation of a launch slip (for example +14 days) or an alternative site for power and Direct-to-Earth communication windows. (4) Educational Mode: a grazing-Sun shadow simulator with CLPS flight case studies. (5) Surface Pathfinder: a 4D rover planner with 3D terrain, slope-hazard layers, A* routing that avoids steep terrain, rover-slip terramechanics, and a one-click EVA flight dossier PDF. (6) Methodology page with formulas, sources and validation. The interface works in English and Spanish, and reports include a bibliography PDF and QR sharing.

How it works. Sun and Earth vectors are computed from the JPL DE421 planetary ephemeris and the NAIF lunar orientation kernel in the Moon's body-fixed frame, including physical libration and light-time correction. Terrain horizons and slopes are derived from the NASA LRO LOLA 20 m/pixel polar DEM (80°S to the pole) and the 128 pixel/degree global DEM. An automated test suite (npm test) and a script that queries NASA JPL Horizons (npm run validate:horizons) show a maximum angular difference below 0.006° across the target sites.

Benefits and intended impact. Mission architects can compare launch dates and sites for power and communications in minutes instead of working from raw ephemerides. Scientists and educators get an interactive way to see why the lunar south pole is uniquely hard. The public can explore real CLPS landing sites with real lighting geometry. The project is open source (MIT) and runs locally with npm install and npm run dev.

Tools and technologies. JavaScript (ES modules), Vite, Three.js (WebGL), jsPDF, qrcode, Node.js test and validation scripts, and a Python data-generation script. Data: NASA LRO LOLA, JPL DE421, NAIF lunar kernels, JPL Horizons (validation).

Creativity. We turned ephemeris tables into things people can see: grazing-Sun shadows, cyclic communication blackouts, and a rover cockpit that plans across space and time. Four data layers (optical, slope, thermal, Earth line-of-sight) explain each hazard in the same view.

Factors we considered. Extreme south-polar lighting (Sun about 1.5° above the horizon), Earth libration of about ±7°, permanently shadowed regions near 40 K, and accuracy against an independent NASA source. For custom coordinates outside the shipped terrain tiles, terrain-derived metrics are reported as N/A unless the user uploads an optional LOLA JSON tile, rather than guessing. Scenario figures in our demo video are illustrative.

Super Intelligence (SI) acknowledgment. The demo video's visuals, animation code and subtitles were generated with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) and carry a visible "SI-GENERATED" watermark. The video's background audio was synthesized programmatically with ffmpeg and is acknowledged here and in the file's metadata.
